title: Theo van Gogh Keeps His Brother Painting
text:
Vincent van Gogh and his younger brother Theo began writing to each other in 1872, when Vincent was nineteen. Theo kept Vincent's letters, and more than six hundred of them survive. They are among the most moving records of an artist's life ever preserved.

Vincent failed as an art dealer, a teacher and a lay preacher before deciding, in 1880, to become a painter. From then on Theo, who worked for the Paris art dealers Goupil and Co., sent him money every month for the rest of his life. It paid for food, rent, paint and canvas. In return Vincent sent his work, which Theo kept and tried, almost entirely without success, to sell. The brothers lived together in Paris for two years, quarreling often; when Vincent left for Arles in 1888, the letters began again.

Theo's support was more than money. He believed in Vincent when no one else did, wrote to him about new art, and was the reader for whom Vincent explained his ideas about color and painting. When Theo's son was born in January 1890, he was named Vincent Willem after his uncle.

Vincent shot himself in July 1890 at Auvers-sur-Oise and died two days later, with Theo at his side. Theo died six months later. They are buried side by side at Auvers. Theo's widow, Jo van Gogh-Bonger, then devoted herself to publishing the letters and showing the paintings.
lesson: Steady faith in someone who is struggling can be worth more than any success. Quiet support, given month after month, may be what keeps another person's work alive.
people: Vincent van Gogh, Theo van Gogh, Jo van Gogh-Bonger
source: Vincent van Gogh, The Letters (Van Gogh Museum edition, 2009)
caveat: Most historians accept that Vincent shot himself, but a minority, notably his biographers Naifeh and Smith, have argued that the shot was fired by someone else.
